comment: What CI holds. One scenario: a request through four behaviours and a handler, which costs
about two hundred nanoseconds — a floor a regression shows up against. The empty pipeline in
SendBenchmarks is deliberately not here: seventeen nanoseconds and a third of movement
between runs of untouched code is a check that cries wolf, and a check that cries wolf gets
ignored.
Two numbers per entrant, and they are not held the same way on purpose.
The ratio is against MediatR in the same run, and not against the hand-written version. The
hand-written one is four private calls the JIT flattens into one, ending at a cached task: it
measures under a nanosecond, the multiple over it is four hundred, and across two runs of the
same code that multiple read 415x and 268x. It stays in the benchmark because it says what
the pipeline costs in absolute terms, and it cannot be a divisor. MediatR does the same work
through a pipeline it builds the same way, on the same machine, in the same run, so it moves
with the runner — and 12.5.0 is frozen under Apache-2.0, so the reference cannot shift
underneath the budget.
The ratios here are the worst of five runs on one machine, not the average. Runtime read
Absolute times drifted across the batch — MediatR alone moved from 249 ns to 346 ns — and the
ratio absorbed most of that but not all of it. Pinning the worst plus fifteen per cent puts
the ceiling above everything seen, which is the point: this half of the budget is the loose
half, and is here to catch something large.
The bytes are the sharp half. Allocation per request is decided by the code and not by the
machine, so it is held as an exact ceiling with no tolerance at all. The regression this
exists for already happened once: the pre- and post-processor behaviours were registered
whether or not a processor existed, costing 110 ns and 480 bytes on every request in every
application through three releases, with the whole test suite green. On this scenario that
would take 688 bytes to 1168 and fail on the first line of the report.
Raising a number here is how a change that is meant to cost something gets agreed. Do it in
the same pull request, never afterwards.
